item.title: How a Thanksgiving Crisis Inspired the Invention of Swanson’s TV Dinner (1953)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” writes New York Times food editor Craig Claiborne. “I am convinced that there are a multitude of people (Americans, mostly, to judge by the people who buy TV dinners and frozen pizzas) who have no taste whatsoever.” That column was published almost exactly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such convenience-oriented food products had already enjoyed prominence in American life for two decades. Though it could hardly have made a dent in the popularity of TV dinners, Claiborne’s typically waspish aside did draw a letter of objection from one Rosalie Levine of Lakewood, California.

“I live alone, I must control my weight. I am not a skilled cook,” she writes. The TV dinner’s price “cannot possibly be bettered”; what’s more, “each oven-ready dinner takes only half an hour’s worth of gas to prepare, and there are no pots or pans to clean up afterward.” While none of these advantages were accidental, the oft-told story of the concept’s emergence begins with a corporate crisis.

“In 1953, someone at Swanson colossally miscalculated the level of the American appetite for Thanksgiving turkey, leaving the company with some 260 tons of frozen birds,” as Smithsonian.com’s Owen Edwards tells it. “Inspired by the trays of pre-prepared food served on airlines,” Swanson salesman Gerry Thomas set the machinery in motion to package the unwanted meat with gravy and sides like cornbread and sweet potatoes, ready for stocking in America’s frozen-food aisles.

The following year, Swanson sold ten million such “TV dinners,” a name attributed to both the shape of the boxes and the form of entertainment families tended to enjoy while eating the meals within. “In 1950, only 9 percent of U.S. households had television sets — but by 1955, the number had risen to more than 64 percent, and by 1960, to more than 87 percent,” writes Kovie Biakolo in a more recent Smithsonian piece. (Among the Smithsonian Institution’s holdings, incidentally, is an original Swanson TV dinner tray.) Another breakthrough came with the introduction of microwave-safe trays, bringing total preparation time under ten minutes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Americans rekindled their love affair with frozen meals, “spending nearly 50 percent more on them in April 2020 over April 2019.”

Where holiday and commercial lore intersect, the details tend to get complicated. Swanson’s TV dinner did have its precedents: the core technology for quick-freezing packaged foods was invented over a century ago by entrepreneur Clarence Birdseye (he of the Birds Eye peas Edwards remembers as “little cryogenic miracles”), and in the late 1940s, different companies planned or attempted to bring frozen meals to market under brands like Strato-Plates, FridgiDinners, and One-Eyed Eskimo. None of those names tapped into the technology transforming not just American mass culture, but also the American way of life. In the fifties, associations with television (and, indeed, with air travel) carried a kind of sophistication they certainly don’t have today. Perhaps Craig Claiborne would be pleased that Americans never quite accepted microwaved TV dinners as a substitute for the Thanksgiving meal; what he’d think of the food they order through their apps is another matter entirely.

item.title: 30 English Phrases for When You Don’t Know What to Say
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

Have you ever been in the middle of an English conversation and suddenly you don’t know what to say?

Maybe someone asks you a question and you need a few seconds to think. Maybe you don’t understand what the other person said. Or maybe the conversation reaches an awkward silence.

The good news is that you don’t need to have the perfect response ready at every moment. Native English speakers experience these situations, too – and we have lots of expressions that help us handle them naturally.

Today I’ll teach you 30 practical English conversation phrases for those moments when you don’t know what to say. These are great expressions to have ready in your mind so that you don’t freeze up when speaking English.

1. When you need a moment to think

Sometimes you understand the question perfectly, but you need a little extra time to formulate your answer in English. Instead of staying completely silent or saying “ummm” repeatedly, try these English conversation phrases.

Let me think for a second.

A simple, natural way to give yourself a few moments to think before responding.

- A: What was the most memorable part of your trip?

- B: Let me think for a second. Probably the day we went snorkeling.

That’s a good question.

You can use this expression to acknowledge someone’s question while giving yourself a little time to consider your answer.

- A: If you could change one thing about your job, what would it be?

- B: That’s a good question. I guess I’d like to have more flexibility.

How should I put this?

Use this when you know what you want to communicate, but you’re trying to find the right words to express it, especially if the topic is complicated or sensitive.

- A: Did you enjoy working with your previous manager?

- B: How should I put this? He was very talented, but he wasn’t particularly good at managing people.

Let me gather my thoughts.

This means you need a moment to organize your ideas before speaking.

- A: What did you think of the presentation?

- B: Let me gather my thoughts. There were some excellent ideas, but I have a few concerns as well.

Nothing comes to mind right now.

Use this when you can’t immediately think of an answer, example, or suggestion.

- A: Can you recommend any good restaurants around here?

- B: Nothing comes to mind right now, but I’ll let you know if I think of one.

I’m trying to find the right words.

This is especially useful for English learners because it lets the other person know that you’re still thinking about how to express yourself.

- A: How did you feel when you finally achieved your goal?

- B: I’m trying to find the right words. It was a mixture of excitement, relief, and disbelief.

2. When you don’t understand something

Don’t pretend to understand something when you don’t! Asking for clarification is a completely normal part of English conversation, even among native speakers.

Sorry, I didn’t catch that.

Use this when you didn’t hear or understand what someone just said, perhaps because they spoke quickly or there was background noise.

- A: We’ll meet at the entrance on the north side of the building.

- B: Sorry, I didn’t catch that. Where are we meeting?

Could you run that by me again?

This is a conversational way to ask someone to repeat or explain something again.

- A: You’ll need to transfer the files before you update the software.

- B: Could you run that by me again?

I’m not quite following you.

Use this when you can hear the words someone is saying, but you’re having trouble understanding their explanation or train of thought.

- A: So technically, we’d save money by spending more money upfront.

- B: I’m not quite following you. How would that work?

What exactly do you mean by that?

Use this when someone’s statement is unclear, vague, or open to different interpretations.

- A: I think we need to take a different approach.

- B: What exactly do you mean by that?

Be aware that your tone of voice is important here. A curious, friendly tone makes this sound like a genuine request for clarification.

Could you give me an example?

Sometimes the easiest way to understand an unfamiliar concept is to ask for a specific example.

- A: You need to make your writing more engaging.

- B: Could you give me an example?

So, are you saying that…?

This is a great way to check your understanding by expressing the other person’s idea in your own words.

- A: We won’t be able to start until everyone has submitted their documents.

- B: So, are you saying that one missing document could delay the entire process?

This technique is particularly useful because it gives the other person an opportunity to confirm or correct your understanding.

3. When you can’t think of a word in English

You might know exactly what you want to say, but there’s one specific English word you can’t remember. Here are some English conversation phrases to handle that situation without abandoning your sentence.

What’s the word I’m looking for?

You can say this out loud when you’re searching for a particular word.

- The instructions were really… what’s the word I’m looking for?… misleading! That’s it.

It’s on the tip of my tongue.

This idiom means you feel that you’re very close to remembering a word, name, or piece of information, but you can’t quite remember it.

- A: Who’s the actor who played the main character?

- B: Oh, I know his name! It’s on the tip of my tongue.

I can’t think of the word, but it’s…

Instead of stopping completely, try describing the thing you’re talking about.

- I can’t think of the word, but it’s a tool you use to remove the skin from vegetables.

The word in this case is “peeler.”

This is an excellent strategy for English learners. You can often communicate successfully even when you don’t know the exact vocabulary word.

For lack of a better word……

item.title: 40 English Phrases For Love, Friendship & Relationships
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

Have you ever met someone and immediately felt comfortable with them? Have you ever lost touch with an old friend, had your heart broken, or fallen head over heels in love?

Relationships are a huge part of our lives, and English has some wonderful expressions for describing the connections we have with other people – from the excitement of falling in love to the challenges of maintaining a friendship.

Today you’ll learn 40 English phrases and expressions about love, friendship, and relationships. Some are simple, everyday phrases, and others are more colorful idiomatic expressions that will help you express yourself more naturally in English.

10 English Expressions About Dating & Falling in Love

1. Have a crush on someone

To have romantic feelings for someone, often without that person knowing about it.

- I had a huge crush on one of my classmates in high school, but I was too shy to talk to him.

2. Ask someone out

To invite someone on a date.

- They’ve been flirting with each other for weeks, and he finally asked her out.

If someone asks you out, there’s generally a romantic intention behind the invitation.

3. Go on a blind date

To go on a date with someone you’ve never met before.

- My sister set me up on a blind date with one of her coworkers.

Notice the expression set someone up with someone – this means to arrange for two people to meet because you think they might be romantically compatible.

4. Hit it off

To immediately like someone and enjoy interacting with them when you first meet.

- We hit it off on our first date and ended up talking for four hours.

You can also use this expression for friendships. It doesn’t necessarily imply romantic attraction.

5. Have chemistry

To have a natural, exciting connection with someone, especially a romantic one.

- They have amazing chemistry. You can tell just by watching them interact.

We sometimes talk about feeling a spark with someone – experiencing that initial feeling of romantic attraction.

6. Fall for someone

To develop romantic feelings for someone.

- I never expected to fall for him, but the more time we spent together, the more I liked him.

This is an informal alternative to saying “fall in love with someone,” although it doesn’t necessarily imply equally deep feelings.

7. Be head over heels in love

To be completely and intensely in love with someone.

- She’s head over heels in love with her new boyfriend. She can’t stop talking about him!

You can also say you’re head over heels for someone.

8. Make the first move

To be the first person to express romantic interest or take action to start a romantic relationship.

- They were both interested in each other, but neither of them wanted to make the first move.

9. The feeling isn’t mutual

This means that one person has romantic feelings for another person, but the other person doesn’t feel the same way.

- He’s really interested in her, but unfortunately, the feeling isn’t mutual. She just sees him as a friend.

The word mutual means shared or experienced by both people. If someone says they like you and you feel the same way, you can say, “The feeling is mutual!”

10. Sweep someone off their feet

To make someone fall in love with you, often in a sudden, exciting, or romantic way.

- He swept her off her feet with his charm, sense of humor, and thoughtful gestures.

Imagine being so impressed or excited by someone that you’re almost lifted off the ground!

10 English Expressions About Friendship

11. Get along well

To have a friendly, positive relationship with someone.

- I get along really well with my neighbors. We often have dinner together.

In British English, you’ll also hear get on well with someone.

12. Have a lot in common

To share many interests, experiences, opinions, or characteristics with someone.

- We have a lot in common – we both love hiking, cooking, and traveling.

Having things in common often helps people form friendships.

13. Go way back

To have known someone for a very long time.

- Sarah and I go way back – we’ve been friends since elementary school.

This informal expression emphasizes the long history you share with someone.

14. Be like two peas in a pod

To be extremely similar to each other in personality, appearance, or behavior.

- Those two are like two peas in a pod. They have the same sense of humor and enjoy all the same activities.

Imagine two little green peas growing next to each other inside the same pod.

15. Be inseparable

To spend so much time together that you’re rarely apart.

- My cousin and I were inseparable when we were kids.

This word can describe close friends, siblings, romantic partners, or even a person and their pet.

16. Keep in touch

To continue communicating with someone, especially when you no longer see each other regularly.

- Even though we live in different countries now, we still keep in touch.

At the end of a conversation with someone you might not see again for a while, you can say, “Let’s keep in touch!”

17. Catch up with someone

To talk to someone you haven’t seen or spoken to recently and exchange news about your lives.

- I’m meeting an old friend for coffee this weekend so we can catch up.

You can also say, “We have a lot of catching up to do!”

18. Be there for someone

To give someone emotional or practical support when they need it.

- When I was going through a difficult time, my friends were always there for me.

If someone is struggling, you can tell them, “I’m here for you.”

19. Have someone’s back

To support, protect, or defend someone, especially in a difficult situation.

- I wasn’t worried about facing the criticism alone because I knew my friends had my back.

This is an informal expression that communicates loyalty and trust.

20. Through thick and thin

Through both good times and difficult times.

- We’ve been friends for over 20 years, and we’ve stuck together through thick and thin.

This expression emphasizes the strength and loyalty of a relationship, even when circumstances become challenging.…

item.title: The Illustrated Version of “Alice’s Restaurant”: Watch Arlo Guthrie’s Thanksgiving Counterculture Classic
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: cultural and historical context

Alice’s Restaurant. It’s now a Thanksgiving classic, and something of a tradition around here. Recorded in 1967, the 18+ minute counterculture song recounts Arlo Guthrie’s real encounter with the law, starting on Thanksgiving Day 1965. As the long song unfolds, we hear all about how a hippie-bating police officer, by the name of William “Obie” Obanhein, arrested Arlo for littering. (Cultural footnote: Obie previously posed for several Norman Rockwell paintings, including the well-known painting, “The Runaway,” that graced a 1958 cover of The Saturday Evening Post.) In fairly short order, Arlo pleads guilty to a misdemeanor charge, pays a $25 fine, and cleans up the thrash. But the story isn’t over. Not by a long shot.

Later, when Arlo (son of Woody Guthrie) gets called up for the draft, the petty crime ironically becomes a basis for disqualifying him from military service in the Vietnam War. Guthrie recounts this with some bitterness as the song builds into a satirical protest against the war: “I’m sittin’ here on the Group W bench ’cause you want to know if I’m moral enough to join the Army, burn women, kids, houses and villages after bein’ a litterbug.” And then we’re back to the cheery chorus again: “You can get anything you want, at Alice’s Restaurant.”

We have featured Guthrie’s classic during past years. But, for this Thanksgiving, we give you the illustrated version.
